Self-Custody & Security

Five Years, Forty Bits: Coldcard Traces 1,779 BTC Theft to One Build Flag

Coinkite’s 18-page incident report traces roughly 1,779 BTC in thefts to a single silent firmware build flag that survived five years and fifteen audits—just as rogue Electrum proxies and a French holder register tighten the screws on self-custody.

No hardware wallet was hacked, no signing device was breached remotely, and no runtime alarm ever went off. That is the chilling core of Coinkite’s 18-page, NTSB-style postmortem published Tuesday and dated November 23, reconstructing how a March 29, 2021 firmware build change set MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG to zero in production—silently swapping the STM32 hardware random-number generator for MicroPython’s software pseudorandom generator across Coldcard Mk2 through Q models for more than five years [s515, s524, s505].

The defect was a silent substitution, not a runtime failure.

Because both interfaces matched, affected Mk2 and Mk3 units quietly generated seeds with roughly 40 bits of effective entropy instead of the intended 128 bits, while Mk4, Mk5, and Q models fell to an unverified estimate near 72 bits [s515]. Attackers eventually brute-forced weak keys offline, draining an estimated 1,778.84 BTC across more than 8,600 addresses starting July 29 before a patch shipped July 31 [s515]. Fifteen independent security reviews over five years—including one that inspected the RNG code weeks before the thefts—missed the build flag [s515]. Coinkite logged roughly 300 loss tickets from 242 accounts as of November 18, has not resolved compensation, and wrote plainly: The losses are real and, for some customers, life-changing. No report or firmware update can undo that. [s515, s524]. Updating firmware does not rehabilitate an old seed; affected wallets must be rotated [s515].

The Coldcard accounting arrived alongside a second live threat to everyday wallet plumbing. Citing researchers 0xB10C and Andrew Toth, Decentralized warned Wednesday morning that more than 30 rogue Electrum proxy servers have moved past passive address surveillance to active theft: they withhold an outgoing transaction and feed back a spoofed replacement whose destination address shares the same trailing characters, tricking users who bump the fee via RBF into signing funds straight to the attacker [s302, s332]. Users are urged to upgrade to Electrum 4.8.3 or newer, inspect full addresses before signing, and point wallets at their own Fulcrum or electrs node [s332].

Toolmakers answered on multiple fronts. Craigraw shipped Sparrow Wallet v2.5.7 (sparrowwallet.com/download), bundling Tor 0.4.9.16, adding testnet5 and narrower window support, fixing sluggish loading on slow Electrum servers, and closing a proxy DNS leak and a balance-hiding glitch identified after a further security review [s6, s329]. OpenSats announced an Unchained donation to its Red Team Fund, with CEO Joe Kelly noting that Strong security doesn’t happen by accident. It comes from researchers who are willing to question assumptions, test critical software, and responsibly disclose what they find. [s68]. Fedi alerted federation users that upgrades to a more decentralised management protocol require moving funds as early as November 30 or by December 15 [s36], and self-hoster A Rux 🚴🏿 shared an LNbits hardening checklist—upgrading past 1.7.1, resetting wallet keys, and replacing full node credentials with scoped runes [s120].

Policy & Surveillance

France Pushes a Wallet Register It Admits Could Endanger Holders

Rapporteurs Mathilde Feld and Nicolas Sansu of France’s Assemblée nationale finance committee have revived a push for a central “FICOBA des cryptoactifs” mapping wallets above €5,000 to named holders, paired with an EU-wide mixer ban and a money-laundering presumption for no-KYC platforms [s104, s511]. In report N° 3291, the lawmakers explicitly concede that such a database constitutes a potential endangerment of those people in the event of a leak like the summer 2026 tax-agency breach—even after French police logged 90 criminal cases and 223 arrests in crypto kidnapping and extortion between January and mid-August, and a French tax official was detained on suspicion of selling investor addresses to criminal gangs [s511].

In Seoul, regulators moved on the exchange layer: South Korea’s Financial Services Commission unveiled a bill capping exchange ownership at 20%, while authorities seek wider freezing powers after locking 11,500 accounts since June [s89, s527].

Markets & Plumbing

Bitcoin Slips Below $60,000 as Tariffs, ETF Exits, and Thin Books Bite

Monday’s Nvidia-driven bounce vanished by Wednesday morning. Markusturm reported bitcoin at $59,073 (€53,974) at 06:20 CET—down 2.4% in 24 hours—while Roger logged $59,327 on daily candles, 53% off October 2025’s $126,199.63 peak, as reports of fresh U.S. tariffs targeting 16 economies rattled equities and pushed November U.S. spot ETF outflows to a record $4.71 billion [s502, s512, s530]. (Wednesday morning figures as of 07:35 CST; not live.)

In “The Collateral Left First,” Roger pointed to a November 21 Canadian print of C$24,250 (~$16,950)—70% below global venues after market makers stepped away—alongside a $16.97 billion four-week contraction in USD stablecoin supply [s530].

A price is not a valuation; it is the last trade that somebody had to do. When the marginal seller is a wrapper that owes dollars by Friday, you are not watching a market vote on the monetary properties of a fixed-supply asset. You are watching a margin clerk work.

Slower money stayed put: Galaxy Research’s Q3 13F tally showed wealth advisors reaching a record 40.5% of institutional ETF holdings over nine straight quarters of net buying while hedge funds fell from 50.6% to 19.0% [s517]. UniCredit opened Italy’s first capital-protected Bitcoin certificate (six years, gains capped at 65%) [s506, s526], Ledn moved U.S. clients onshore with custody accounts [s520], and the DOJ moved to forfeit $1.1 billion in frozen USDC from October’s Binance hack [s521].

World & Energy

Hormuz Hits Day 269 as Tanker Freight Touches 9.2× Normal

The Strait of Hormuz entered its 269th day of effective commercial closure this week, with just one vessel transiting on November 22 against a pre-crisis norm near 85 per day [s516]. At the ELNET Jerusalem Summit on November 23, former Mossad director David Barnea dismissed diplomatic talks with Tehran and called for regime change, while Iran’s army commander ordered the navy to tighten the strait further [s516].

Economist Jim Bianco argued that Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have created a crude surplus beside a diesel bottleneck that joins bipartisan U.S. trade barriers to lock in goods inflation [s514]. On Nostr, builder A Rux 🚴🏿 launched Maritime Outlook (maritime.ruxit.tech), a self-hosted dashboard pricing tanker freight futures against Brent crude at 9.2× its 2023–2025 average, with attack tallies unlocked for 100 sats per 30 days or via L402 APIs [s164, s134].

Supply & Law

One in Ten “Lost” 2018 Wallets Has Moved

Revisiting 92,076 addresses already dormant six-plus years in 2018, developer Quickben22 found that 9,990 of them—10.8%—have since spent roughly 245,000 BTC ($14.7 billion), while over 2.26 million BTC stays untouched [s513]. The data undercuts the “five-year silence equals abandonment” claim in a live New York lawsuit targeting 39,069 dormant addresses [s513].

Artificial Intelligence

Did AI’s Jevons Paradox Just Break?

Corporate spend stalls, “zero retention” springs leaks, and Signal shuts out agents.

Corporate card data from Ramp cooled the infinite-demand thesis. Co-CEO Eric Glyman told Garry Tan that over the last two months, Jevons paradox broke for AI, with OpenAI and Anthropic spend growth dropping from ~40% to 1–2% while the top 1% of firms drive 80% of volume [s518]. Anthropic stock slipped under its $83 IPO price to $75.85 [s502].

Hosted privacy cracked too: Coincards.com flagged an Ars Technica test where two million canaries caught “zero data retention” AI pipelines leaking user prompts, alongside breaches at Bell, Samsung Securities, and Cleverbridge [s72, s64, s90, s111]. The EFF backed Signal’s move to block AI agents [s160], and Ken 🎋 noted reported intrusions at FinCEN, the CIA, and ODNI [s273].

Builders split on what stays valuable: hodlbod wrote that PCs, more powerful than ever, have instantly become no more than a "dumb terminal" used for accessing industrial intelligence. [s234], while Cameri🐲 favored cheaper open models [s349], Hag₿ard migrated a smart home in 90 minutes on self-hosted Qwen [s21], and Sebastix marked Alex Dergachev’s closing line on mglaman.dev: Technology is getting commoditized. Human nature isn't. [s495].

Builders & Software Desks

One-click Tor relays, digital hankos, and Android apps
Self-Hosted & Tools

Give Bandwidth Back, Cut Out the Middleman

Running a Bitcoin node over Tor is common; donating bandwidth back to the network is less so. A Rux 🚴🏿 announced that two packages they maintain—Snowflake, a safe-from-home proxy for censored users, and a non-exit Tor Relay—have landed in the official Start9 marketplace as one-click StartOS installs [s258]. Their own home Snowflake proxy has relayed 344 GB for users across 79 countries led by the United States, Iran, and Russia, while their VPS relay has pushed 338 GB since October 29 [s258]. Freedom.Tech’s privacy desk added that Tor Browser 16.0.3, Tails 7.18, and Mullvad Browser 16.0.3 all shipped in sync, alongside SimpleX Chat’s Trail of Bits audit and a pool-host memory fix in NerdQAxe+ 1.1.3-rc.1 [s504].

Elsewhere in the workshop, modulo unveiled Digihan (digihan.org), a free open-source replacement for AdobeSign modeled on Japanese hanko seals: hash a document, sign it with your Nostr key, anchor the timestamp via opentimestamps.org, and embed a scannable proof without an intermediary [s129]. Erik shipped Zeile 1.2 (zeileapp.com), adding end-to-end encryption to his two-person home-screen doodle app—no accounts. no feed. no followers. no likes. no streaks. [s70, s75]. Tuma shared sv2blocks.com to track Stratum V2 mainnet blocks [s295], and Blockstream demonstrated how a Jade hardware wallet can store a multisig descriptor to recover a 2-of-3 Sparrow quorum even if both a key and its backup file are lost [s312].

Craft & Season

Lino Stamps, Pond Ice, and Black Friday Friction

As the holiday shipping rush turns ugly—BitcoinBrabant advised customers not to order during Black Friday after a courier arrived four hours late reporting more than ten times normal parcel volume, leaving one package lost and another perched atop a letterbox [s136]—makers leaned into slower hands. Tynka finished hand-printing December envelopes with hand-cut lino stamps, calling it So satisfying to be in charge of the whole process. [s168]. In Sicily, SatsOil was filling tins of its second olive harvest [s206].

Outdoors, Sondre traded snowboarding and wakeboarding for early-winter pond hockey despite rough skate edges [s183, s250], BitBees spotted two shrimp boats preparing for Thanksgiving [s303], and Rustypuppy noted November’s full Beaver Moon—hidden behind complete cloud cover [s279]. Rosetta polled the network on whether Christmas lights belong up before Thanksgiving [s441], and five readers traded WORD5 #782 grids—with Max Trotter and Nestking solving it in two [s23, s88, s91, s233, s324].

Notebook

From the Amazon, a Memory Crutch, and a Quiet Ward

Tim Bouma posted a brief good-night from the Amazon jungle over Starlink [s294, s319], while closer to home two quieter posts cut through the noise. GoldfishThumb1 reflected candidly on struggling with memory offline—forgetting names, instructions, even exits—and relying on Nostr’s durable written timeline to keep track of relationships: In that sense, Nostr is a sort of mental crutch for me. [s154]. And Reid Walley wrote four devastating lines about his mother, who used the word “derrière” her whole life and never once said “butt”: When nurses and doctors use the word butt, Mom doesn’t know what they mean. Now, thanks to dementia, she no longer recognizes “derrière” either [s7].
